Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The writer effectively alternates between dramatized real-time scenes and compressed exposition to maximize the emotional impact of the narrative. The central event—attending the synagogue service, recognizing the shooter, the shooting itself, and the chaotic rush out of the sanctuary—is rendered in vivid, real-time scenes with sensory details, dialogue, and physical action (e.g., Ruth touching Barbara's stomach, the sound of the congregation gasping, the crowd pushing Barbara backward). 

At the same time, the writer skillfully uses summary and exposition to provide vital context without bogging down the pacing. The flashback to Camp Tamarack concisely establishes Barbara's prior connection to both Rabbi Adler and the troubled boy, making the climax deeply personal. Similarly, the final section uses summary to compress the weeks and years following the tragedy—covering the rabbi's death, the birth of Barbara's son, and her lingering guilt—allowing the story to reach a poignant, reflective resolution.
